source: A charge crossing a uniform field moves like a projectile: steady across, accelerated sideways.
Students use the voltage itself as the field, forgetting to divide by the plate gap.

A charge crossing a uniform field moves exactly like a ball thrown sideways under gravity: steady along the plates, accelerated across them. The same splitting as Horizontal Launches works. Each problem here is one short scene and a chain of questions. Answer them in order: each later question uses what you found before, so a slip early on carries through. Keep full precision between steps and round only at the end.
$$E = \frac{V}{d}, \qquad a = \frac{qE}{m}, \qquad t = \frac{\ell}{v_0}, \qquad y = \tfrac{1}{2}at^2.$$ An electron is pulled toward the positive plate; gravity is far too weak to matter.
Between the plates the path is a parabola; after them it is a straight line.

An electron at $2.0 \times 10^7\ \text{m/s}$ enters plates $4.0\ \text{cm}$ long, $2.0\ \text{cm}$ apart, with $100\ \text{V}$ across them. Find (1) the field, (2) the time inside and (3) the deflection.
Using $V$ where $E$ belongs. The field is volts per meter: divide by the gap in meters. Check units: $qE$ must come out in newtons.
